# Protocol audit — results

*Generated by `analyze_audit.py` from `coding.csv` (19 included papers). Coder: AI (mentor); the researcher's blind double-coding (`reliability_order.txt`) and Cohen's κ are still pending, so these shares are **provisional**.*

## Planned shares (Wilson 95% CIs)

| Quantity | k/n | Share | 95% CI (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| (a) compares at a fixed number of retrieved chunks (`fixed_k`) | 12/19 | 63% | [41, 81] |
| (a') budget-matched (`fixed_budget` or `both`) | 1/19 | 5% | [1, 25] |
| (b) reports the amount of retrieved text | 2/19 | 11% | [3, 31] |
| (b') controls text amount (budget, matched lengths, or chunker-independent unit) | 6/19 | 32% | [15, 54] |

| (d) evaluates on more than one dataset | 13/19 | 68% | [46, 85] |
| (e) headline claim exposed to the text-amount confound (exposed, with or without text reported) | 9/19 | 47% | [27, 68] |

## Candidate artefacts: headline claims comparing arms of different chunk length at a fixed number of chunks

We do **not** claim these conclusions are wrong; only that the protocol leaves the text-amount confound uncontrolled for the quoted claim (PROTOCOL.md 'Output').

| Paper | k | Headline claim | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bhat2025chunksize` | 1,2,3,4,5 (analysis focuses on k=1) | "smaller chunks (64-128 tokens) are optimal for datasets with concise, fact-based answers, whereas larger chunks (512-1024 tokens) improve retrieval in datasets requiring broader contextual understanding" (p. 1, Abstract) | Arms are fixed chunk sizes 64/128/256/512/1024 tokens compared by Recall@k with the same k, so at k=1 the 1024-token arm retrieves 16x the text of the 64-token arm. Two embedding models; four of six datasets are stitched synthetic documents. |
| `muthyam2026ragstability` | 2,3,4,5 | "The strongest EM configuration in the baseline grid was chunk size 120 with top k=3, for both rerank off and rerank on." (p. 6, Sec. 5.3) | Full factorial chunk size {80,100,120,140} x top-k {2..5} x rerank; packed generation context capped at ~452 tokens, which partly bounds text at generation but not at retrieval (Hit@k at equal k). Packed token counts reported (Table 4 by k; Fig. 5). SD across 3 seeds only for noise/stability runs; chunk-size contrasts have no uncertainty. Single dataset. |
| `beyondchunkthenembed2026` | 10 (rank cutoff for DCG@10 / nDCG@10) | "optimal chunking strategies are task-dependent: simple structure-based methods outperform LLM-guided alternatives for in-corpus retrieval, while LumberChunker performs best for in-document retrieval" (p. 1, Abstract) | In-document task ranks chunks with a fixed cutoff (DCG@10) and counts a chunk relevant on any overlap with a gold paragraph, so larger chunks gain both coverage and relevance. In-corpus task is document ranking via MaxP (text amount not the retrieved unit). Explicitly treats chunk size as a possible confound (RQ4) via per-query correlations of chunk size with effectiveness (r up to 0.44 in-document), but does not equalise retrieved text. Paired t-tests vs best/worst. |
| `chunkembedsensitivity2026` | 5 | "content-aware chunking significantly improves retrieval effectiveness over naive fixed-length splitting" (p. 1, Abstract) | 36 strategies whose chunk sizes range from 50-token windows to paragraph groups, all compared at top-5. Each retrieved chunk is graded by an LLM judge for support of the reference answer, so longer chunks have more chances to be judged relevant. Notes that 'average chunk length alone is an incomplete predictor' (p. 10) but does not equalise or report retrieved text per strategy. nDCG CI bounds are computed (p. 11) but no pairwise tests are shown for the headline 'significantly' claim. |
| `garrido2026chunksize` | NA (reciprocal rank of first relevant chunk) | "no single chunk size consistently outperforms others across all mediums. Instead, the effectiveness of a given chunk size is tied to the structure of the text." (p. 8, Conclusion) | Count-based rank metric (RR) over chunks of sentence/paragraph/page/chapter granularity; a chunk is relevant if an LLM judges that it contains the answer, so larger chunks are more often relevant. Text amount not controlled. Says 'significantly outperformed' without any test. Generation quality is motivated but not evaluated. |
| `chunkingcost2026` | 5 (Accuracy@5), 10 (Recall@10); 5 for generation (capped at 4,000 tokens) | "Methods with fewer but more coherent chunks (e.g., GraphSeg and Lumberchunker) achieve the strongest Recall@10 and Accuracy@5 ... chunk quality and structural coherence are more important than chunk quantity" (p. 7, Sec. 4) | States explicitly that chunk sizes were not normalised across methods (p. 4). Relevance = chunk overlaps the answer span. The headline attributes the advantage of methods producing fewer (hence longer) chunks to 'coherence', while comparing at equal k: a direct instance of the uncontrolled text-amount confound. Generation context capped at 4,000 tokens. Failed configurations excluded (T/S markers). |
| `queryadaptivechunking2026` | 5 | "QASC achieves an F1-score of 0.85, representing a relative improvement of 18-27% over fixed chunking baselines" (p. 1, Abstract) | Fixed chunking at 150/300/500/700/1000 tokens and variable-length adaptive chunks, all compared at top-5. A chunk counts as relevant if it contains at least one needed sentence, which favours longer chunks. SDs over 5-fold splits of the 40 queries; the introduction mentions 'significance testing' (p. 2) but no test is reported in the text. Coded seeds_only as the closest category (fold-to-fold variability). |
| `jimenoyepes2024financial` | 10 | "Findings support that element type based chunking largely improve RAG results on financial reporting." (p. 1, Abstract) | Top-10 for every strategy; base chunks of 128/256/512 tokens vs element-based chunks that the authors note are 'closer in size to Base 512' (p. 8), i.e. larger than two of the baselines. Reports chunk counts, not retrieved text per strategy. Page-level accuracy is evaluated from retrieved chunks, so larger chunks cover more pages' text at equal k. |
| `duarte2024lumberchunker` | 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 (DCG@k, Recall@k) | "LumberChunker not only outperforms the most competitive baseline by 7.37% in retrieval performance (DCG@20) but also that, when integrated into a RAG pipeline, LumberChunker proves to be more effective than other chunking methods" (p. 1, Abstract) | Mean chunk lengths are reported (Table 9): LumberChunker 334 tokens vs Semantic 185, Paragraph 79, Proposition 12, Recursive 399, but all are compared at equal k, so e.g. at k=1 LumberChunker retrieves ~4x the text of paragraph chunks. Recursive chunks are longer than LumberChunker's and still score lower, so length does not explain every contrast. No uncertainty. |
